title: How Markets and Accounts Work
intro: Before choosing what to buy you need to know where and how it trades: who is on the other side, what an order actually does, what you pay in visible and hidden costs, and which kind of account to hold it in.

blocks.text: Primary and secondary markets

Companies and governments raise money in the primary market: a company sells new shares in an initial public offering (IPO) or later offering, and a government sells new bonds at auction. After that the securities change hands between investors in the secondary market, which is what people usually mean by 'the stock market'. When you buy a share of a large company on an exchange, your money goes to the seller, not the company. Secondary markets matter to companies all the same: a liquid market with a fair price is what lets them raise money in the first place.
Exchanges, brokers and market makers

An exchange (the New York Stock Exchange, Nasdaq, the London Stock Exchange, the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Euronext and others) runs an order book that matches buyers with sellers. You reach it through a broker, a firm licensed to place orders on your behalf and to hold your securities. Market makers stand ready to buy and sell continuously, quoting a bid (the price they will pay) and an ask or offer (the price they will sell at). The difference is the bid-ask spread, and it is a real cost: buy at the ask and sell at once at the bid and you lose the spread.

Large, heavily traded stocks have spreads of a cent or so; small stocks, corporate bonds and exotic funds can have spreads of 1% or more. Many US retail brokers send orders to wholesale market makers who pay for the order flow, which is how 'commission-free' trading is funded; the cost is hidden in the execution price, though for small orders in liquid stocks it is usually small.

Bonds and currencies mostly trade over the counter (OTC): dealers quote prices to clients directly rather than through one central order book. That makes prices less visible to small investors and spreads wider, which is one reason most individuals hold bonds through funds.
Orders

items: Market order: buy or sell now at the best available price. It always fills, but the price can be worse than you saw, especially in thin markets or at the open.
Limit order: buy at no more than (or sell at no less than) a set price. You control the price but might not trade.
Stop order (stop-loss): becomes a market order once the price falls to (for a sell) a trigger level. In a fast fall or overnight gap it can fill far below the trigger.
Stop-limit order: becomes a limit order at the trigger, so it won't fill at a terrible price, but it may not fill at all.
Time in force: a day order expires at the close; good-'til-cancelled stays open until filled or cancelled.

blocks.text: For a long-term investor buying a fund, a limit order at or slightly above the current ask during normal trading hours is a simple way to avoid paying a bad price in a sudden spike.
Settlement, custody and protection

A trade is agreed at once but settles (cash and securities actually swap) a little later: one business day after the trade (T+1) for US stocks since May 2024, and T+2 in many other markets. Your broker holds the securities for you, usually in 'street name'. In the US, the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC) protects customers up to \$500,000 (including up to \$250,000 of cash) if a broker fails and securities are missing, though not against market losses; other countries have similar schemes (the UK's FSCS, for example).
Margin and short selling

A margin account lets you borrow from the broker against your holdings. With \$10,000 of your own and \$10,000 borrowed you hold \$20,000 of stock: a 10% rise gains you 20%, and a 10% fall loses you 20% (plus interest). If losses push your equity below the maintenance margin (often 25 to 30% of the position) you get a margin call and must add cash or be sold out, often at the worst moment. Leverage multiplies volatility, and through volatility drag it can lower the long-run compound return even when the average return looks higher.

Short selling is selling borrowed shares, hoping to buy them back cheaper. The most you can make is 100% (if the price goes to zero); the most you can lose is unlimited. You also pay a borrowing fee and any dividends the shares pay while you are short. A short squeeze happens when rising prices force short sellers to buy back, pushing the price higher still.
Indexes

An index is a basket that tracks a market. The S&P 500 holds about 500 large US companies weighted by market value; the Dow Jones Industrial Average holds 30 weighted by price (an old method with odd effects); the Nasdaq Composite is tech-heavy; the Russell 2000 covers small US companies. Abroad: the FTSE 100 (UK), DAX (Germany), CAC 40 (France), Nikkei 225 and TOPIX (Japan), Hang Seng (Hong Kong), and global indexes such as the MSCI World and MSCI ACWI (All Country World Index, which adds emerging markets). In bonds the Bloomberg US Aggregate is the usual benchmark. Index funds and ETFs copy these baskets.

Most stock indexes are market-cap weighted: each company counts in proportion to its total market value (share price times shares outstanding, usually counting only shares that are freely traded, the free float). This means the biggest companies dominate: in recent years the ten largest US stocks have made up over a third of the S&P 500.
Kinds of account
Where you hold an investment can matter as much as what you hold, because of taxes. The details are country-specific; the shapes are similar everywhere.

items: Taxable brokerage account: no limits or lock-ups, but dividends, interest and realized gains are taxed each year.
Tax-deferred retirement account (US: traditional 401(k) and IRA; UK: pension/SIPP; Canada: RRSP): contributions reduce taxable income now, growth is untaxed, withdrawals are taxed as income later.
Tax-free account (US: Roth IRA and Roth 401(k); UK: ISA; Canada: TFSA): contributions come from taxed money, but growth and qualified withdrawals are tax-free.
Education and health accounts (US: 529 plans, HSAs) with their own rules.

Employer match: many US employers add money to your 401(k) when you contribute, often 50 to 100% of the first few percent of salary. That is an instant return no investment can match, and taking it in full is usually the first step.

blocks.text: Accounts come with yearly contribution limits, early-withdrawal penalties and rules that change. The Taxes, Costs and Pitfalls page goes further.
Before you invest at all

items: Pay off high-interest debt first: paying off a credit card at 24% is a sure 24% return.
Keep an emergency fund, typically three to six months of spending, in cash or a high-yield savings account or money market fund, so you never have to sell investments in a downturn.
Know your time horizon for each goal. Money needed within about five years generally belongs in cash or short bonds, not stocks.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: The cost of a spread
blocks.text: A small-cap stock is quoted 9.90 bid, 10.10 ask. You buy 1,000 shares at the ask and later sell at the bid when the quote hasn't moved. What did the round trip cost, as a percentage?
solution: You pay \$10,100 and receive \$9,900: a \$200 loss, about 2% of the mid price of \$10.00. That is a cost you pay whenever you trade, before any commission.

blocks.title: Margin call
blocks.text: You buy \$20,000 of stock with \$10,000 of your own and \$10,000 borrowed. The broker's maintenance margin is 30% of the position's value. How far can the stock fall before a margin call?
solution: Equity is the value $V$ minus the \$10,000 loan; the call comes when $(V - 10000)/V = 0.30$, so $V = 10000/0.7 \approx \$14{,}286$.
That is a fall of $1 - 14286/20000 \approx 28.6\%$. A fall of 28.6% in the stock wipes out 57% of your equity.

blocks.title: Short squeeze arithmetic
blocks.text: You short 100 shares at \$50. The price rises to \$120 before you buy back. What is your loss, and how does it compare with the most you could have made?
solution: Loss $= 100 \times (120 - 50) = \$7{,}000$, plus fees. The most you could have made was \$5,000 (if the stock went to zero). Losses on a short have no ceiling.
